newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole exchange opening shots in TV debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole exchange opening shots in TV debate.

text.p: President Bill Clinton opened the first presidential debate on Sunday by extolling his record in office and promising to extend it while Republican Bob Dole presented himself as a plain-speaking man whose word could be trusted.

"Four years ago you took me on faith, now there's a record," Clinton said in his opening statement at the 90 minute debate less than one month before the Nov. 5 election. "We are better off than we were four years ago. Let's keep it going."

"Well, he may be better off," Dole quipped when given a chance to reply to Clinton's claim, getting a laugh from the audience in Hartford's Bushnell Theater. He went on to take a jab at the president by saying that such American foes as Iraqi President Saddam Hussein may also be better off but said Americans were not.
Clinton shot back that Americans were indeed better off economically and in other ways and said Dole had acknowldeged as much in the past.

In his own opening statement, which followed Clinton's, Dole used his two minutes to try to present himself personally to a public that, polls indicate, he has not yet connected with as well as he would like.

"I'm a plain-speaking man and I learned long ago that your word was your bond, and I promise you tonight I'll try to address your concerns and not exploit them," he said, addressing the television audience.
